passage: Note from Keerthana, playgroup teacher. Sahil, two, arrived tearful and stood at the door with his blanket, then lifted both arms to me until I picked him up. He clung, thumb in mouth. Later a boy near us cried over a bumped knee, and Sahil toddled over and patted his shoulder, copying the way I had patted him. I think he was tired and unsure this morning; the patting looked like imitation of care, though he may have felt something for the boy too.

qa.q: What did Sahil do when he arrived at the playgroup door?
qa.a: He stood with his blanket, then lifted both arms until Keerthana picked him up.

qa.q: What does Sahil's clinging with his thumb in his mouth suggest, and what else could explain it?
qa.a: It suggests he was tired or unsure and needed comfort. It could also be simply his usual way of settling in.

qa.q: What could Keerthana do to help Sahil's next morning arrival?
qa.a: Keerthana can greet him at the door, let him keep his blanket, and stay close for a while before he joins the others.

qa.q: How might the boy with the bumped knee experience Sahil's pat?
qa.a: He may feel noticed and a little comforted, even though Sahil was probably copying more than understanding his pain.

grounding: A toddler reaches up, clings and holds a blanket for comfort, and pats a crying peer in imitation of care.

passage: At the well in the village, Pankaj's neighbour's little girl started to cry when her bucket tipped. Hrithik, two, put down the blanket he carried everywhere and walked over. He patted her arm, saying "Aa, aa," the way his father pats him. Then he returned to Pankaj, lifted his arms, and pressed his face to his father's shirt, rubbing the blanket on his cheek.

qa.q: What did Hrithik do when the girl's bucket tipped and she cried?
qa.a: He put down his blanket, patted her arm and made a soothing sound.

qa.q: What does Hrithik's return to his father with raised arms suggest, and what else might it mean?
qa.a: It suggests he needed comfort himself, perhaps because the crying upset him or he was tired. It could also be just a wish for closeness.

qa.q: How could Pankaj respond to Hrithik?
qa.a: He can pick him up, hold him quietly, and say something simple like the crying scared you, then let him settle. 🤍

qa.q: How might the crying girl feel about the pat?
qa.a: She may feel a bit comforted that someone noticed, though Hrithik is probably copying his father's pat rather than fully grasping her upset.

grounding: A toddler pats a crying peer in imitation of care and seeks comfort himself by reaching up and holding a blanket.

passage: I am Vaibhav, and I was in the shop when I saw two toddlers by the toy shelf. Indu, about two, grabbed a red car out of another child's hands. He wailed. Her father knelt and said gently, "Say sorry, Indu." She muttered, "Sorry," and pushed the car back into the boy's hand, then patted his arm. I doubt she knew she had done wrong, but her hand was gentle.

qa.q: What did Indu take from the other child?
qa.a: She grabbed a red car.

qa.q: What does Indu's gentle pat after returning the car suggest, and what else could explain it?
qa.a: It suggests she wanted to make things better after her father's prompt. She may only have been copying, without understanding that she had upset the boy.

qa.q: What could Indu's father do next to help her learn?
qa.a: He can keep showing simple repair, like giving the toy back and offering a hug, and say the boy felt sad without heavy blame.

qa.q: How might the boy feel when Indu pats him?
qa.a: He may feel comforted to have his car back, but he might still feel upset for a while.

grounding: A toddler who grabbed a toy hands it back and gives a gentle gesture after a prompted sorry, showing early reparation.

passage: On Monday Tanvir, two, snatched a truck from his cousin. Sudha said, "Tanvir, sorry?" and he handed it back, looking at the floor. On Wednesday he grabbed a spoon from his cousin and, when she cried, gave it back and flung his arms round her, without any prompt. On Friday he took her cup again and only gave it back when Sudha reminded him. Sudha thought the giving back was growing, though the grabbing was not gone yet.

qa.q: What did Tanvir do on Wednesday when his cousin cried?
qa.a: He gave back the spoon and hugged her without being told.

qa.q: What might Tanvir have felt when he handed back the truck on Monday, and what else could explain it?
qa.a: He may have felt uneasy because Sudha's tone changed and his cousin was upset. He may also just have been following her instruction, without seeing his own fault.

qa.q: What could Sudha do to support Tanvir's progress?
qa.a: Sudha can keep prompting simply, notice warmly when he repairs, and not expect him to stop grabbing all at once. 🙂

qa.q: How might Tanvir's cousin experience these three days?
qa.a: She probably feels upset when things are taken, but the hug and returned toys tell her he cares.

grounding: A toddler offers a toy back or a hug after prompting, showing early reparation rather than understanding of fault.

subtype: Likes and dislikes as strong assertions [Expressing]
passage: Note from Kalyani, nursery teacher. At snack Ritu, two, pushed the banana away, saying "No!" and pointed hard at the orange slices. When another child picked up her cup she shouted "Mine!" and gripped it with both hands. Ritu is strongly sure of what she likes. It may also be the end of a long morning. I said, "You want the orange and you want your cup," and gave the oranges. She calmed and ate.

qa.q: What did Ritu point at after refusing the banana?
qa.a: She pointed hard at the orange slices.

qa.q: What does Ritu's insistence on the cup suggest, and what else could it be?
qa.a: It suggests she is developing strong preferences and independence. It could also be tiredness at the end of a long morning.

qa.q: What could Kalyani do in the future when Ritu refuses food?
qa.a: Kalyani can name what Ritu wants and offer choices where she can, and stay calm when a refusal is firm.

qa.q: How might the child who reached for the cup feel?
qa.a: The other child may be surprised and a bit upset by the shout, and would need help finding their own cup.

grounding: A toddler shows likes and dislikes by refusing food and saying mine and no, expressing growing independence.

subtype: Likes and dislikes as strong assertions [Expressing]
passage: Minakshi placed a plate of rice and dal in front of Bhavna on the verandah in the village. "No!" Bhavna shoved it a hand's width away and pointed at the roti on her mother's plate. Minakshi gave her a piece. Then the neighbour's hen wandered near the plate and Bhavna cried "Mine!" and held it close, though she had refused it a moment before. Minakshi laughed, quietly, and let her eat.

qa.q: What did Bhavna want from her mother's plate?
qa.a: She wanted a piece of roti.

qa.q: Why did Bhavna suddenly claim the plate when the hen came near?
qa.a: She probably felt her own things were being threatened and wanted to protect her choice. It could also just be the excitement of the hen's arrival.

qa.q: What could Minakshi try to make meals easier?
qa.a: She can offer a couple of foods and accept some refusals without a fuss. 😊

qa.q: How might Bhavna's refusal look to a passing neighbour?
qa.a: It might look like naughtiness, but it can also be understood as a toddler asserting her taste and independence.

grounding: A toddler shows likes and dislikes by refusing food and saying mine, a sign of independence.

subtype: Toddler cries, points and single words [Expressing]
passage: Under the neem tree, Jatin, two, began to cry, fists tight. His mother Amandeep checked in turn. "Hungry?" She held out a piece of roti; he pushed it away. "Thirsty?" He drank a little and kept crying. Then he rubbed his eyes and dropped his head on her shoulder. "Sleepy," she said, and rocked him. If the crying kept up or worried her, she would ask the doctor, but this time he slept.

qa.q: What did Jatin do when Amandeep offered the roti?
qa.a: He pushed it away.

qa.q: What does Jatin's rubbing his eyes and dropping his head suggest, and what else might the crying have meant?
qa.a: It suggests he was tired and needed sleep. The same crying could also have meant thirst or discomfort, which is why Amandeep checked each.

qa.q: What is a good way to respond to an unclear toddler cry?
qa.a: Check the likely needs one after the other, such as food, drink, sleep and comfort, and see a doctor if it keeps going or worries you.

qa.q: What might Jatin have felt when his first signals were not understood?
qa.a: He may have felt frustrated, since the roti and water did not fit what he needed.

grounding: A toddler cries, pushes away and rubs eyes, and the adult checks needs in turn.

subtype: Toddler cries, points and single words [Expressing]
passage: On the Sydney ferry Chidi, two, started whimpering and pointed at his father's bag. "More," he said. Jin handed him a cracker; Chidi threw it on the deck and wailed. Jin offered water, which Chidi pushed away. Then Chidi tugged at his ear and lay against Jin's arm, eyes half closed. "You're tired," said Jin softly, and held him. If it went on or worried him, he would check with a doctor.

qa.q: What did Chidi say when he pointed at his father's bag?
qa.a: He said "More."

qa.q: What might Chidi's tugging his ear and half-closed eyes suggest, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: They suggest he was tired and wanted to rest against his father. Tugging an ear can also signal discomfort, which is why Jin would check with a doctor if it kept up.

qa.q: What could Jin do to help Chidi settle?
qa.a: He can keep holding him quietly and give him time to sleep, having ruled out food and water for now. 🙂

qa.q: How might a passenger see the wailing?
qa.a: They may think it is simply a fussy child, but Jin's calm checking shows the cry had a real need behind it.

grounding: A toddler signals need with crying, pointing and pushing away, and the same cry can mean several needs that adults check in turn.

passage: At the bus stop outside the village, Nirmala, two, wanted to ring the conductor's bell. Her father Gurpreet said, "Not now." Nirmala threw her water bottle and then sank to the ground, limp and whining. Gurpreet crouched. "You're cross. You wanted the bell." He did not give in, but stayed beside her. After a while she wiped her eyes, took his hand and climbed onto the bus.

qa.q: What did Nirmala throw when her father said not now?
qa.a: She threw her water bottle.

qa.q: What does Nirmala's going limp suggest she was feeling, and what else might explain it?
qa.a: It suggests frustration at being told no, since she wanted the bell. It could also be tiredness from the wait for the bus.

qa.q: What worked in Gurpreet's response?
qa.a: He held the limit calmly, named her feeling and stayed close instead of giving in or scolding.

qa.q: How might other passengers see Nirmala's protest?
qa.a: Some may see a spoiled child, but others will recognise a tired toddler with a blocked wish.

grounding: A toddler protests by throwing and going limp, and it improves with a calm limit and a nameable feeling.

passage: In a Seoul flat, Paulo, two, was told by Soo-ah it was time to leave the blocks and get dressed for the park. "No!" He hurled a block, whined and flopped on the floor. Soo-ah waited a breath, then sat near him. "You wanted to keep building. It's hard to stop." She took his hand firmly. "Blocks stay here, we come back later." He sniffed, then let her help him with his shoes.

qa.q: Why was Paulo told to leave the blocks?
qa.a: He had to get dressed to go to the park.

qa.q: What does Paulo's throwing and flopping suggest, and what else might be behind it?
qa.a: It suggests frustration because his play was stopped. He might also have been tired or hungry, which makes stopping harder.

qa.q: What could Soo-ah do to help him next time?
qa.a: Soo-ah can give a warning before stopping and promise when he can play again, then stay calm as she did. 😊

qa.q: How might Soo-ah feel when Paulo throws a block?
qa.a: Soo-ah might feel a flash of stress, but the calm reply shows Soo-ah understands it as a big feeling.

grounding: A toddler protests with whining, throwing and going limp, and improves with a calm limit and a named feeling.

passage: On Sunday Suraj, two, tired after a long visit, bit his cousin's arm when she took his ball. Naveen stepped in and lifted him away. "No biting. You're tired and cross." On Tuesday Suraj grabbed a book and shoved his friend, and Naveen said, "Stomp, don't push," and stomped himself until Suraj copied. The next Saturday, a toy was taken, Suraj's face crumpled, and he stomped hard, shouting "Mine!" instead of biting.

qa.q: What did Naveen suggest Suraj do instead of pushing?
qa.a: He said, "Stomp, don't push," and stomped himself until Suraj copied.

qa.q: What might Suraj have felt when he bit his cousin, and what else could explain it?
qa.a: He probably felt a strong wave of anger or tiredness with no words for it. It may not have been meant to hurt, only to stop the loss of his ball.

qa.q: What can an adult do when a toddler bites or hits?
qa.a: Step in to keep everyone safe, name the feeling in a few words, and show a safer action to try.

qa.q: How might the cousin have felt after the bite?
qa.a: She may have been hurt and upset, so she needs care too.

grounding: A toddler grabs, hits or bites from frustration or tiredness, and adults step in, name the feeling and show a safer action.

passage: In the Pune playschool, Damini, two, saw another girl take her doll. She hit the girl's arm and screamed. Tanvir knelt between them. "I won't let you hit. You're angry, you wanted your doll." He held Damini's wrists gently and said, "Hands can pat, or hands can squeeze me." Damini squeezed his fingers hard and sobbed. The other girl handed the doll back, watching her warily.

qa.q: What did Damini do when the other girl took her doll?
qa.a: She hit the girl's arm and screamed.

qa.q: What does Damini's hard squeeze of Tanvir's fingers suggest she was feeling, and what else could it be?
qa.a: It suggests strong anger or hurt that she could not put into words. It could also be that she felt overwhelmed by the noise around her.

qa.q: What did Tanvir show her that she could do with her hands instead?
qa.a: He showed her she could pat or squeeze his hand, a safer way to let out the feeling.

qa.q: How might the other girl feel as she returns the doll?
qa.a: She may feel frightened or unsure, and would also need a calm word from an adult. 🤍

grounding: A toddler who lacks words hits when frustrated, and the adult steps in, names the feeling and shows a safer action.

passage: In the village courtyard Sabina, two, ran to her father Karthik holding out her knee. "Ouch! Fell!" she said, pointing at a purple bruise. He crouched and looked closely without fuss. "You fell on the step. That must have hurt." She nodded, and he kissed his hand and touched the spot. If it seemed to worry her more or kept bothering her, he would show the doctor. She wandered off to play.

qa.q: What did Sabina show her father?
qa.a: She showed him a purple bruise on her knee.

qa.q: What does Sabina's running to her father suggest, and what else might she have wanted?
qa.a: It suggests she trusts him and wanted him to notice what happened. She may also have wanted comfort or attention as much as care for the knee.

qa.q: How does Karthik's calm response help Sabina in the long run?
qa.a: It teaches her that telling him what happened leads to warmth, so she is more likely to confide later.

qa.q: How might Sabina feel about telling him?
qa.a: She probably feels heard and relieved, which is why she ran off to play afterward.

grounding: A toddler shows a bruise and points out what happened, and the adult responds calmly.

passage: At a Cape Town park a large dog barked from behind a fence. Lucia, two, dropped her spade and ran to Thabo, gripping his trousers. "Scared," she said, in a small voice. Thabo lifted her. "The dog barked loudly. That was scary." She pointed at the fence. "Dog," she said. "Yes, a dog, behind the fence. I've got you." Her grip slowly loosened and she looked at the fence again.

qa.q: What word did Lucia use to tell Thabo how she felt?
qa.a: She said "Scared."

qa.q: What does Lucia's pointing at the fence suggest, and what else might it mean?
qa.a: It suggests she is trying to tell Thabo what caused her fear and is starting to make sense of it. She might also be checking whether the dog is still a danger.

qa.q: How did Thabo's response help?
qa.a: He stayed calm, named the fear and the cause in a few words, and held her, so she felt safe telling him.

qa.q: What might Lucia learn if Thabo had laughed at her fear?
qa.a: She might feel embarrassed and be less likely to tell him when she is frightened later. 🙂

grounding: A toddler says scared and points out what happened, and calm adult response encourages later confiding.

passage: On Tuesday Ujjwal hid his face behind a blanket and popped out. "Peek-a-boo!" Kishore, eighteen months, shrieked with laughter and pulled the blanket to his own face. On Friday Kishore's aunt tried the same from the doorway. He stared at her without a smile and reached for Ujjwal. Next Sunday, Ujjwal crossed his eyes and blew a raspberry, and Kishore giggled and demanded "Again, again!"

qa.q: How did Kishore react to Ujjwal's peekaboo on Tuesday?
qa.a: He shrieked with laughter and pulled the blanket to his own face.

qa.q: What does Kishore's stare at his aunt suggest, and what might be another reading?
qa.a: It suggests he does not feel as safe with her yet, so the surprise was not fun. He could also just have been in a quieter mood that day.

qa.q: What could Ujjwal do to help the aunt join the game?
qa.a: He can let the aunt sit nearby first, then join in gently, and let Kishore lead.

qa.q: How might Kishore see the game with Ujjwal?
qa.a: He probably enjoys knowing the pattern and being surprised, and feels safe with the person playing it.

grounding: A toddler laughs at peekaboo and silly faces and repeats the game, and the delight depends on a safe, familiar partner.

passage: In the kitchen of their flat, Sharmila covered her face with a dish towel. "Where's Minakshi?" she said in a funny voice. Minakshi, nearly two, giggled and kicked her legs. Sharmila dropped the towel. "Boo!" Minakshi shrieked and grabbed for it, wanting more. Then the doorbell rang and a stranger looked in, making a face. Minakshi's smile disappeared and she stared, then reached for Sharmila.

qa.q: What did Sharmila use to hide her face?
qa.a: She used a dish towel.

qa.q: What does Minakshi's smile disappearing when the stranger looked in suggest, and what else might it mean?
qa.a: It suggests the surprise was unwelcome coming from someone unfamiliar. She might also have been startled by the sudden bell.

qa.q: What could the visitor do differently?
qa.a: The stranger can wait, smile softly from a distance and let Minakshi warm up before playing. 🙂

qa.q: How does the game feel to Minakshi with Sharmila?
qa.a: It feels safe and fun, since she knows what comes next and Sharmila's voice and face are familiar.

grounding: A toddler laughs at peekaboo and surprises, but the delight depends on a safe, familiar partner.

passage: On Monday Ujjwal, two, held a banana to his ear and said, "Hello, Mama!" Parveen laughed and took the "call." On Wednesday she told him, "Hop like a bunny!" and he hopped, delighted. On Saturday a neighbour said, "It's raining cats and dogs." Ujjwal ran to the window, looked at the sky, and asked, "Cat? Dog?" Parveen said, "It's raining a lot." He looked unconvinced.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal use as a telephone on Monday?
qa.a: He used a banana.

qa.q: What does Ujjwal's question at the window suggest, and what other reading is there?
qa.a: It suggests he took the idiom literally and looked for cats and dogs in the sky. He might also just have been playing along.

qa.q: What could Parveen do with a toddler when using sayings?
qa.a: She can say what she means in plain words and enjoy pretend games together.

qa.q: How does the neighbour see what happened?
qa.a: The neighbour probably meant nothing but the weather and may find it funny that a small child took her words at face value.

grounding: A toddler understands words literally and uses a banana as a phone, enjoys hopping like a bunny, but takes an idiom at face value.

passage: "Hold your horses, Hemant," said Raghav, as the boy tugged at his shirt at the flat door. Hemant, two, looked around the hall. "Horse?" he asked. "No horse, I mean wait." "Horse gone." Later he picked up the TV remote, put it to his ear and said, "Hello, Papa?" Raghav answered the call. Then Raghav said, "Hop like a frog," and Hemant hopped in circles, giggling.

qa.q: What did Hemant use as a phone?
qa.a: He used the TV remote.

qa.q: What does Hemant's search for the horse suggest, and what might be another reading?
qa.a: It suggests he took the saying literally and thought Raghav meant a real horse. He might also have been copying the word without much understanding.

qa.q: What could Raghav do to help Hemant?
qa.a: Raghav can say plainly what he means and keep the pretend games, which Hemant enjoys.

qa.q: How might Hemant see Raghav's answering the remote call?
qa.a: He probably feels understood and enjoys sharing the pretend with Raghav. 😊

grounding: A toddler understands words literally and pretends an object is a phone, enjoys hopping like an animal, but idioms mean nothing yet.

passage: On Friday evening Nandini, two, sat near the little lamp at home and folded her hands like her mother Farida, eyes darting around. On Tuesday at a neighbour's singing evening she clapped along, a beat behind. On Sunday, at a relative's gathering, she watched everyone bow and bent her head down to the ground too, then looked up, grinning. Farida guessed Nandini was copying more than believing, and simply enjoyed belonging.

qa.q: What did Nandini do at the singing evening?
qa.a: She clapped along, a beat behind the others.

qa.q: What might Nandini's grin after bowing suggest, and what else could it mean?
qa.a: It suggests she enjoyed doing what everyone else did and felt part of the group. She could also just have liked the bending game.

qa.q: How could Farida respond to Nandini's imitation?
qa.a: She can welcome her joining in without pushing or explaining too much, and enjoy that Nandini feels included. 🙂

qa.q: How might relatives see Nandini's bow?
qa.a: They may find it sweet and feel that the child is joining the family's practice.

grounding: A toddler folds hands, claps and bows like her family, expressing belonging and imitation rather than belief.

passage: Every evening Pradeep rang the small brass bell during the family's lamp time in their Chennai flat, and Chaitanya, two, stood beside him with a toy bell. He shook it hard, clapped when Pradeep clapped, and folded his hands a moment before running off. One evening he shook his bell at the goldfish bowl instead. Pradeep smiled. "Bell for the fish?" he asked, and let it be.

qa.q: What did Chaitanya do with his toy bell during lamp time?
qa.a: He shook it and stood beside Pradeep, clapping when Pradeep clapped.

qa.q: What does Chaitanya's ringing at the fish bowl suggest, and what else might it mean?
qa.a: It suggests the bell is a fun sound to him more than a solemn act, as he copies Pradeep's actions. It could also mean he was bored that evening.

qa.q: How does Pradeep's smile help Chaitanya?
qa.a: It tells him that joining in is welcome and safe without pushing him to do it a certain way. 🙂

qa.q: How might Pradeep see Chaitanya's copying?
qa.a: He probably sees it as belonging and imitation, and enjoys having him beside him at that time of day.

grounding: A toddler rings a bell, claps and folds hands like his family, expressing imitation and belonging rather than belief.
